transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. To start, can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well… I guess what brings me in is I just don’t have the get-up-and-go like I used to. I used to be in choir, and I’d do my quilting, and I’d go visit folks… you know, Mrs. Carter always liked when I came by, though her house had those funny little curtains—anyway, now most days I just sit at home with the TV turned down low. People are expecting me places, I know they are, but I just can’t seem to push myself to go.
How long have you been feeling this way—weeks, months, or longer?

Oh… longer than weeks, definitely. It kind of started building after I retired from the school office—must be a little over two years now. I used to know everybody’s children’s names there, and who needed lunch forms, and then after I left it got quiet at home… so, yes, I’d say a couple years, bit by bit.
Have you noticed any changes in your memory or ability to concentrate, like forgetting recent conversations or getting confused about familiar tasks?

Memory? Hmm… I don’t know. I mean, I misplace things sometimes, but everybody does, don’t they? My glasses will be right on the side table and I’ll swear I put them in the kitchen. But I still know my way around my house and the usual things.

Concentrating… I suppose I don’t sit with things as long as I used to. I’ll start watching a program and then the commercials come on and I remember the laundry, or that I meant to call somebody, and then—well, I don’t always do it. But I can’t say I’ve been forgetting whole conversations or getting mixed up doing familiar things, not that I’ve noticed.

Over these past two years, has your low mood stayed pretty much the same low level the whole time, or have there been certain weeks or months where it got noticeably worse—like feeling much more hopeless, losing interest in everything, or changes in sleep and appetite—followed by times when you felt more like your usual self?

I don’t rightly know how to separate it out like that. It’s been… mostly just me being low and slow, I suppose. Some days are worse, sure, like when it rains and the house feels too quiet, or when I think I should call someone and then I don’t. But weeks or months where it’s a whole different thing and then I’m back to myself? I’m not sure I’ve noticed it that way.

My sister used to say you can tell a person’s mood by whether they open the curtains in the morning—she had these yellow curtains, terrible to wash, caught every bit of dust—anyway, I guess I don’t keep track close enough. It’s just been sort of… going on.
Over these past two years, have you noticed changes in your sleep—like trouble falling asleep, waking up too early, or sleeping much more than usual?

Sleep… well, I can’t say I’ve kept proper track of it. Some nights I’m in bed and I’m thinking about whether I locked the back door, or if I left a dish soaking, and then I remember my mother used to say never leave knives in the sink—she was very particular about that.

But as for falling asleep or waking early… I don’t know if it’s different enough to say. I have some nights that aren’t good, I suppose, but I haven’t really noticed a clear change like sleeping all day or anything I could measure.
Over these past two years, have you noticed any changes in your appetite or your weight—eating noticeably more or less than usual?

Appetite… I don’t know. I eat when I remember to, mostly. Some days it’s toast or soup, and other days I’ll make eggs if I feel up to washing the pan after. My aunt used to keep biscuits in a tin by the stove—one of those blue tins, not for sewing like people do now—and I was thinking I should get one like that, but then I forget when I’m at the store.

As for weight, I haven’t really been watching it. My clothes seem about the same, I think. Nothing I’ve noticed in a big way.
Over these past two years, have you ever felt like you were worthless or excessively guilty about things, or had thoughts that life wasn't worth living?

Worthless… I don’t know. I get to thinking I’m not much use these days, with not working and all, but then a lot of people my age aren’t, are they? My neighbor used to say retirement is just “being put on the shelf,” which I never liked—she had all those little glass birds on her shelf, always dusting them.

Guilty, well… I think about things I didn’t do, people I didn’t call, but I don’t know if that’s “excessive.” And life not worth living… I’m not sure how to answer that. I’ve felt tired of things being the way they are sometimes, but I don’t know that I’d put it like that.

Has there ever been a stretch of at least two weeks where you lost interest or pleasure in almost everything—even things you used to enjoy, like choir or quilting—every single day, not just some days?

Yes… I suppose that’s what’s been going on, more or less. I used to have more push for things—choir, quilting, going to see people—but now most days I just stay home. I’ll leave the TV on low, not really watching it, just so the house isn’t so quiet.

People expect me places sometimes, and I know they do… choir practice and such, or someone saying I should come by. But I just don’t get myself up and going like I used to. I wouldn’t know if it’s exactly every single day for two weeks, but it’s been most days for a good while.
Thinking back over these two years, has there been any stretch of two months or longer where you felt back to your normal self, with your energy and interest returning, before things got low again?

I don’t think so, not two months where I felt like my old self. It’s been sort of building since I retired from the school office, which was… a little over two years ago now. Funny, I can still picture the front counter there, the little bell people would tap even when I was sitting right there.

But no, I can’t think of a good long stretch where my energy and interest came back proper and then went away again. It’s more like it’s just been sliding that way since I stopped working.
Over these past two years, have you generally felt low in energy or unusually tired nearly every day, even when you haven't been doing much?

Yes… I mean, I don’t seem to have the push I used to. I used to go to choir, work on quilting, visit folks, and now most days I’m just at home with the TV on low. Not really watching, just there in the room.

People expect me places, I know they do, and I think, well, I should get up and go… but then I don’t. It’s like I can’t get myself started. My mother used to say “once you put your shoes on, you’re halfway there,” but half the time I don’t even get to the shoes.
Have you ever had thoughts of wanting to hurt yourself, or wished you wouldn't wake up, during this time?

I… I don’t know how to answer that exactly. I don’t think I’ve sat and made plans to hurt myself, if that’s what you mean.

Sometimes I wake up and think, “Oh, another day,” and then I just lie there a while. But wishing not to wake up… I’m not sure. My aunt used to say mornings were the hardest after she got older, because the house makes all its little noises and you start thinking about everything. I suppose I get like that too sometimes, but I wouldn’t say I’m trying to do anything to myself.
Over these past two years, have others noticed you moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or alternatively, have you felt unusually restless or fidgety, nearly every day?

I’m not sure… I don’t really watch myself that way. My daughter might say I take longer getting my words out, but then she’s always in a hurry, you know? She talks fast, like my sister used to when we were girls.

Restless… no, I don’t think of myself as fidgety. I sit a lot. But whether it’s “nearly every day,” I couldn’t say. I haven’t paid much attention to that.
Before this period after your retirement, had you ever gone through a similar stretch of low mood, low energy, or loss of interest earlier in your life?

I don’t know… earlier in my life, I suppose everybody has sad times, don’t they? When my children were little there were hard patches, money and all that, and my husband’s work schedule was never steady. I remember one winter the pipes froze and we all had to stay with my cousin, and she had this little dog that barked at every spoon dropping—

But as far as a stretch like this, like after I stopped working… I’m not sure I can say. I didn’t think of it in those terms back then. I just kept going because there were things that had to be done.

During this time, has your low mood and lack of energy ever gotten so severe that you had trouble managing basic daily things—like keeping up with meals, bathing, or paying bills—or has it mostly stayed at a level where you could still manage those things, just with less enthusiasm?

I can still do the little daily things, mostly. I mean, I eat something, I wash up… the bills, I don’t like them, but who does? My husband used to keep them in a cigar box, and I still have that box somewhere, though it doesn’t smell like cigars anymore.

But I did have to step back from some things. I used to help lead the choir, and over at the senior center I’d say I could help with a project, and then I just wouldn’t keep up with what I promised. That embarrassed me. People from church check on me more now than they used to, calling or stopping by like they’re making sure I haven’t dropped off the map. So… I manage at home, but not like before with other things.

Well… like I was saying, I still get by at home, but I did have to give up some things. The choir, mostly—I used to help lead, and I liked that, you know, the hymns we’d do at Christmas, everybody standing too close together in the little room—

But I couldn’t keep up like I said I would. Same with little projects at the senior center. I’d tell them I’d help, and then it would just… not get done. That made me feel bad. And now people from church call or stop by more, like they’re checking I’m alright. So I suppose it has changed things some.

I know I’m repeating myself a bit… but yes, it’s mostly those outside things that slipped. The choir, I had to step back from helping lead it. I used to keep track of who was singing what, and then I just couldn’t keep up with what I’d said I’d do.

And the senior center too—little projects, nothing grand, but I’d promise I’d help and then it would sit there. Makes me feel foolish. Church friends call more now, or stop by, like they’re making sure I’m still managing. They’re kind about it, but I notice.

Yes… I think it’s changed things, just not so much with feeding myself or washing up. It’s more that I had to step back from leading the choir. I used to keep track of things, and then I’d say I’d do something and not keep up with it.

Same with the senior center projects. Little things, you know, like helping sort papers or set up something—I’d mean to do it, but then it wouldn’t get done. And now folks from church call or come by more than they used to, like they’re checking on me. They’re sweet about it, but I can tell.

I suppose the main thing is I’ve had to pull back from the choir. I used to help lead it, keep track of who was doing what, and I liked that… especially around holidays, you know, when everyone wants the old songs done just so.

But I’d promise things and then not keep up. Same with the senior-center little projects—I’d say, “Yes, I can help with that,” and then it would just sit. So now I don’t take on as much. And people from church call or stop by more than they used to, kind of checking on me. They mean well, I know they do.

Well… like I said, I don’t do as much at church now. I used to help lead the choir, and I enjoyed that, keeping track of the songs and who was doing what, but then I’d say I’d take care of something and it just… wouldn’t happen.

And at the senior center, same sort of thing. I’d agree to help with a little project, nothing big, and then I couldn’t keep up with what I promised. So I’ve had to step back some.

People from church, they’re kind, they call or stop by more now. I think they’re checking on me, though they don’t say it that way.

I guess it’s mostly the choir and the senior center things. I used to be the one who helped keep the choir together—well, not all by myself, but I knew the hymns, and I liked when we’d practice for Christmas, because my mother used to sing those same songs in the kitchen.

But lately I’d say I was going to handle something, and then I just wouldn’t keep up with it. Same with little projects at the senior center. So I stepped back. And now the church ladies call more, or stop by with some excuse, but I know they’re checking on me. They’re kind about it, though.

I used to be in choir, and I’d do my quilting, and I’d go visit folks… you know, Mrs. Carter always liked when I came by, though her house had those funny little curtains—anyway, now most days I just sit at home with the TV turned down low. doctor.intent: Determine the duration of this low motivation/interest to differentiate an acute depressive episode from a chronic persistent condition
doctor.question: How long have you been feeling this way—weeks, months, or longer?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been building since I retired from the school office, a little over two years ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the main problem of low motivation and reduced activity has been going on.

patient.answer: Oh… longer than weeks, definitely. It kind of started building after I retired from the school office—must be a little over two years now. I used to know everybody’s children’s names there, and who needed lunch forms, and then after I left it got quiet at home… so, yes, I’d say a couple years, bit by bit.

doctor.intent: Assess for cognitive decline (memory, concentration, confusion) to distinguish a mood disorder from a neurocognitive disorder
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your memory or ability to concentrate, like forgetting recent conversations or getting confused about familiar tasks?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about memory, concentration, forgetting conversations, or confusion with familiar tasks, which are cognitive concerns not covered by the listed symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Memory? Hmm… I don’t know. I mean, I misplace things sometimes, but everybody does, don’t they? My glasses will be right on the side table and I’ll swear I put them in the kitchen. But I still know my way around my house and the usual things.

Concentrating… I suppose I don’t sit with things as long as I used to. I’ll start watching a program and then the commercials come on and I remember the laundry, or that I meant to call somebody, and then—well, I don’t always do it. But I can’t say I’ve been forgetting whole conversations or getting mixed up doing familiar things, not that I’ve noticed.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the low mood has been continuously present at a mild-to-moderate level for the past two years, or whether it has occurred in distinct, more severe episodes separated by periods of more normal mood
doctor.question: Over these past two years, has your low mood stayed pretty much the same low level the whole time, or have there been certain weeks or months where it got noticeably worse—like feeling much more hopeless, losing interest in everything, or changes in sleep and appetite—followed by times when you felt more like your usual self?
